sections.heading: Understanding Color Spaces and Why They Matter
paragraphs: HEX and RGB describe colors in the sRGB color space, which is the standard for screens, web browsers and most digital design tools.
HSL represents the same color as a combination of hue, saturation and lightness, making it more intuitive for designers who think in terms of how a color looks rather than how it is encoded.
CMYK is the color model used in print, and while the picker does not output CMYK directly, knowing the RGB value lets you approximate the printed result using conversion formulas.
Understanding which color space your target output uses prevents surprises when a color that looks perfect on screen prints with a noticeably different tone.

sections.heading: Sampling Strategies for Accurate Color Extraction
paragraphs: A single pixel may represent a highlight, shadow or compression artifact rather than the intended color of the object, so sampling a small area and noting the dominant value produces more reliable results.
Zooming into high-resolution images reveals fine detail that casual viewing misses, especially in photographs with subtle gradients or textured surfaces.
When the image contains noise or grain, clicking several nearby pixels and comparing their values helps you identify the true color rather than a random fluctuation.
For images with anti-aliased edges, sampling from the center of a color region avoids picking up blended transitional pixels that do not represent either adjacent color accurately.

sections.heading: Extracting Palettes for Design Systems and Tokens
paragraphs: Modern design systems define colors as semantic tokens that map to specific HEX or RGB values across light and dark themes.
The color picker lets you extract each token value from a brand photograph, mood board or competitor screenshot, then record them directly into your design token file.
Building a palette from real imagery rather than guessing produces a more cohesive visual language that feels grounded and intentional.
Once the tokens are defined, they propagate automatically through CSS variables, component libraries and style guides, maintaining consistency everywhere the design appears.

sections.heading: Color Picking for Accessibility Compliance
paragraphs: Accessible design requires sufficient contrast between text and background colors, and the picker gives you the exact values needed to calculate contrast ratios.
Extracting the foreground and background colors from a design mockup and checking them against WCAG guidelines ensures that the final product meets accessibility standards.
Colors that appear distinct on a large monitor may have insufficient contrast for users with low vision, making the numerical check essential rather than optional.
Pairing the extracted values with a contrast-checking tool completes the accessibility workflow from extraction to validation.

sections.heading: Using Extracted Colors in CSS, Sass and Tailwind
paragraphs: HEX values paste directly into CSS custom properties, while RGB values work well in functions that require separate red, green and blue channels.
Sass variables accept any of the three formats, letting you choose the notation that best matches your project conventions.
Tailwind CSS uses a configuration file where custom colors are defined as HEX or RGB strings, and the picker output formats map directly to those definitions.
Having the color in the right notation at extraction time eliminates the extra conversion step that slows down implementation.

sections.heading: Working With Low-Resolution and Compressed Images
paragraphs: Social media thumbnails and compressed email attachments often lose color fidelity through JPEG artifacts, making the sampled value less accurate than the original.
Recognizing the limitation of low-resolution sources prevents you from encoding a slightly wrong color into your design system.
When possible, extracting from the highest-resolution version of the image available produces the most trustworthy color values.
For archived or legacy images, noting that the color came from a compressed source helps future maintainers understand why a value may not match the original intent.

faqs.q: Which color formats does the picker return?

faqs.q: Can I enlarge parts of the image for precise picking?
faqs.a: Yes. The picker supports zooming into the photo so you can select exact pixels without guesswork.

faqs.q: Is the color picker private and free?
faqs.a: Yes. All processing happens locally in your browser with no uploads, watermarks or accounts.

faqs.q: How do I ensure the color I pick matches the intended design?
faqs.a: Sample from the center of a color region rather than edges or anti-aliased boundaries, and use high-resolution source images when available for the most accurate result.

faqs.q: Can the extracted color values be used for accessibility checks?
faqs.a: Yes. The HEX and RGB values returned by the picker can be entered into contrast-ratio calculators to verify compliance with WCAG accessibility guidelines.
